title: Value embeddings on every layer (FLOP-free capacity)
description: has_ve() now returns True for all layers: 6 -> 12 value-embedding tables (25.2M -> 50.3M params, 71.3M -> 96.5M total) at identical FLOPs/token.
reflection: NEGATIVE / wash: val_bpb 0.987221 vs baseline 0.986277, i.e. +0.0009 -- right at the noise floor, so at best a tie and certainly not a win. The mechanism worked exactly as predicted and that is what makes the result informative: FLOPs/token was literally unchanged (3.460393e8 both ways) and the throughput cost was small (331.5M -> 322.3M tokens, -2.8%; MFU 38.5% -> 37.4%; peak VRAM 32.1 -> 33.0 GB). So this was a near-free +25M parameters, and it bought nothing. Doubling depth-wise VE coverage -- including finally giving layer 0 a value embedding, which the alternating pattern denied it -- did not move the loss. Conclusion for the group: the round-4 read that 'we are at compute-optimal size' is too narrow. It is not that added capacity costs too many tokens; added capacity does not help even when it is free. These are sparse embedding params: with ~322M tokens over an 8192-token vocab each row sees plenty of updates, yet the extra per-layer tables are redundant with what the residual stream already carries. The alternating VE pattern is not load-bearing either -- it is simply not a lever in either direction. Remaining ideas I would rank above another capacity variant: WINDOW_PATTERN (attention span is untested and trades ~9% FLOPs for full context), and schedule shape (WARMDOWN_RATIO 0.5 is a guess nobody has probed). I would not spend a slot on VE-on-first-half as I earlier suggested; with the all-layers version flat, that sub-axis has no headroom.
